summary:
Magdalena department stands under the national framework of Colombia. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, Congress passed a law banning discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in 2011, and Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement. Since a rule change approved in June 2015 a trans Colombian changes the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a declaration before a notary; the earlier route, in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments, no longer applies. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Same-sex marriage has been available since April 2016, full adoption rights for same-sex couples since 2015, and transgender people have been permitted to serve openly in the armed forces since 2015.

No finding specific to Magdalena on law, enforcement practice, facilities or incidents affecting trans people appears in the sourced material. The reference article on Magdalena Department records no department-specific trans finding, and national reporting on attacks against LGBTQ+ people published on 6 August 2025, after the killing of Sara Millerey, carries no Magdalena-specific information either.

The national baseline a visitor is assessed against is lethal violence. Colombia recorded 41 trans women killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and 13 trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video circulated showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja stated that "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

Some of that targeting is organised. The Guardian reported on 30 July 2024 that armed groups in Caquetá gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers against trans women; the same investigation quotes an activist stating that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide and records the killings as ordinary cases. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, listing trans people among those described as military targets. Caquetá and Guajira stand as department-level examples of a documented national pattern; the sources supply no equivalent reporting for Magdalena.

Protection machinery exists and has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with killings rising.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to facilities and custody are governed by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (guards at a Cali mall) and T-301 of 2004 (police at the Santa Marta boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since ruled on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
tangentialFactors:
Colombian society is described as generally conservative on LGBT issues. An Invamer poll of October 2019 recorded 50% support for same-sex marriage for the first time, with 47% opposed. The poll is national, dated 2019 and offers no reading on opinion within Magdalena department.

Colombia was the fourth Latin American country to legalise same-sex marriage when the Constitutional Court did so in April 2016, a comparative standing that places its formal framework ahead of most regional peers while the violence data runs in the opposite direction.

Reporting on the killings frames them as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict, and the 2023 transitional-justice indictment treats conflict-driven attacks on LGBTI people as gender persecution. Armed-group activity, kill-list flyers and "social cleansing" campaigns in departments such as Caquetá and Guajira belong to that conflict setting rather than to ordinary street crime, which matters for how a visitor reads risk outside major cities.

The UN Human Rights Committee has noted concern over the pattern of violence, and the May 2025 UN fact-finding mission found widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention. Both are external assessments of Colombia as a whole, not findings about Magdalena.

outOfScopeNotes:
No department-specific sourced material on Magdalena exists in this inventory. Two of the four sources state the absence directly, and the remaining two are national in scope. Everything in the summary about law, enforcement, facilities and violence describes the national framework the department stands under, not conditions documented within it.

Whether Magdalena has local police protocols for hate incidents, accessible gender-affirming care, trans-led organisations or a record of prosecutions for attacks on trans people is not sourced here and remains unverified.

Judgment T-301 of 2004 concerns police conduct at the Santa Marta boardwalk. The sources do not state the geographic relation of that city to Magdalena department, so its weight as a local data point is unresolved.

The violence figures rest on media reporting and an encyclopaedic reference rather than primary statistical publications; the 41 killings in 2023 and the eight recorded between February and April 2024 could not be reconciled against a single official series in this inventory.

The Attarney General's Office count of 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025 is not broken down by victim gender identity, and the 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 comes from a separate count.
